chapter: Harlem, 52nd Street and the first big bands
title: Billie Holiday, Lady Sings the Blues and the Hazel Scott incident
summary: He met Holiday at the Alexander Bar, doubts the book's version of a Famous Door incident, and suggests it was mixed up with a firing of Hazel Scott for sitting with a white patron.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them
story.community_name: Billie Holiday as the musicians knew her

blocks.x: Did you get to know Billie, Billie Holiday, there, or you just heard her there?

Oh, well, I met her there, but I didn't really get to know her until later, later on. But in fact she was the one that reminded me of it. She said, "You know, the first time I saw you," and she recalled it, and I said, "Oh, my goodness. That's right, that was you."
She -- you've read, "Lady Sings the Blues?"
Was that the way it happened, in the
Well, I don't know. I mean something happened there. Of course -- let's put it this way. Roughly that is about the way it happened, but when you smooth it out it isn't exactly that way.
You -- I know this is not like in chronological order, but since you've mentioned Billie Holiday, do you want to tell us how it happened?
I really don't remember. I don't remember it happening in the way it was described in 'Lady Sings the Blues.'
I know there was a scene there, and exactly what happened, it's gone. But to me, I don't think the way it was put in the book is exactly the way it happened.
Well, sometimes those things, as told to, get twisted around a little bit.
Yeah, because something like that had happened with Hazel Scott, too.
For what, for sitting at a table with you, or -- which is what Billie says happened.
Yeah. And that's why I've often wondered if somebody didn't get the two stories mixed up. Now, I can't tell you which way or who or what, but those things did
happen. There was definitely a no-no, I mean to be overly friendly with a black person at that time.
